additions.reason: The shofar is the structural archetype that anchors the entire Torah. Its physical form — narrow at the mouth (below), wide at the bell (above) — is the template for the proper pattern of awakening from below. The Rebbe explicitly calls the awakening from below 'בִּבְחִינַת שׁוֹפָר'. It is a neutral structural object (an instrument/body-part analogue) that serves as a bechina for positive spiritual practice; it has no evil polarity in this Torah.
additions.source_quote: בִּבְחִינַת שׁוֹפָר, שֶׁהָרָחָב הוּא לְמַעְלָה וְהַקָּצָר הוּא לְמַטָּה אֵצֶל הַפֶּה

additions.reason: The awakening from below is the central spiritual practice described in this Torah. It IS (bechina) the shofar pattern: narrow at the bottom (beginning from distress/compression) and opening wide above. The Rebbe explicitly equates it with the shofar shape using bechina language.
additions.source_quote: וְכֵן בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִלְּמַטָּה, צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מִלְּמַטָּה קָצָר, בִּבְחִינוֹת: וְדִבֶּר פִּי בַּצַּר לִי, בִּבְחִינַת שׁוֹפָר

additions.reason: The verse 'my mouth spoke in my distress' (Psalms 66:14) is used as a bechina of both the shofar shape and the proper awakening from below. It names the pattern: the speaking (פֶּה) is at the narrow/compressed side. The Rebbe explicitly frames it with 'בִּבְחִינוֹת' twice — first introducing it as the embodiment of the shofar principle, then stating it again as the destination of the teaching ('וְזֶה בְּחִינוֹת: וְדִבֶּר פִּי בַּצַּר לִי').
additions.source_quote: וְזֶה בְּחִינוֹת: וְדִבֶּר פִּי בַּצַּר לִי, הַיְנוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַצַּד הַצַּר וְהַקָּצָר אֵלַי, אֵצֶל פִּי, בִּבְחִינוֹת שׁוֹפָר כַּנַּ"ל

additions.reason: The narrow place / distress (מֵצַר, also called צַר or צָרָה in the text) is the experiential reality corresponding to the narrow lower end of the shofar. It is structurally equivalent (bechina) to 'בַּצַּר לִי' and to the mouth-end of the shofar. It is neutral in polarity — not itself evil, but the condition of constriction that serves as the proper starting point for upward movement. David's troubles with Absalom and Naval are examples.
additions.source_quote: שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה הָיָה מִן הַמֵּצַר וְהַדֹּחַק, שֶׁהָיָה צַר לוֹ מְאֹד

additions.reason: David's prayers beginning from the narrow place (מֵצַר) are the concrete embodiment of the shofar / awakening-from-below principle. The prayer that begins from distress and arrives at ruach hakodesh IS the shofar pattern in action. Specifically, the starting point (מן המצר) is a bechina of the shofar's narrow mouth; the arrival at ruach hakodesh is the eitza destination (not a bechina).
additions.source_quote: שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה הָיָה מִן הַמֵּצַר וְהַדֹּחַק... וְאַחַר־כָּךְ בָּא בְּאוֹתוֹ תְּפִלָּה לְתוֹךְ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ

additions.reason: The divine spirit / holy inspiration is the destination that David's prayers from distress arrive at. In the structure of this Torah it corresponds to the wide upper end of the shofar — the expanded spiritual state reached after starting from the narrow place. The relationship to מֵצַר is EITZA (distress produces/leads to ruach hakodesh), not bechina — they are not two expressions of the same thing. Ruach hakodesh is included here because it is a significant concept in the Torah but its connection to the shofar cluster is directional (eitza), not parallel (bechina).
additions.source_quote: וְאַחַר־כָּךְ בָּא בְּאוֹתוֹ תְּפִלָּה לְתוֹךְ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ

additions.reason: The pattern of Torah teaching that begins broad below and narrows as it rises. This is one of two structural archetypes described in sentences 1–2. The Rebbe does not use explicit bechina language to equate these two patterns with each other or with the shofar, but they are clearly the structural background from which the shofar teaching emerges.
additions.source_quote: יֵשׁ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים תּוֹרָה מִלְּמַטָּה לְמַעְלָה, וְהִיא מִלְּמַטָּה רְחָבָה מְאֹד

additions.reason: The pattern of Torah teaching that begins broad above and narrows as it descends. The inverse archetype to the first pattern. Together these two archetypes (sentences 1–2) set up the structural framework for the shofar teaching in sentence 3.
additions.source_quote: יֵשׁ לְהֵפֶךְ, שֶׁאוֹמְרִים תּוֹרָה מִלְּמַעְלָה לְמַטָּה, וְשָׁם לְמַעְלָה הִיא רְחָבָה מְאֹד מְאֹד

additions.reason: The holy spark — what remains at the very top of the 'Torah from below upward' pattern after all the narrowing. This concept anchors the positive value of even a very compressed teaching: above, 'there is certainly some holy spark' (כִּי בְּוַדַּאי יֵשׁ שָׁם אֵיזֶה נִיצוֹץ הַקָּדוֹשׁ). It is good in polarity.
additions.source_quote: כִּי בְּוַדַּאי יֵשׁ שָׁם אֵיזֶה נִיצוֹץ הַקָּדוֹשׁ

additions.reason: David is cited as the paradigmatic example of one who prays from the narrow place (מֵצַר) and arrives at ruach hakodesh. His name is not given a bechina label but he functions as the personification of the שׁוֹפָר / הִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִלְּמַטָּה principle.
additions.source_quote: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ אֵצֶל דָּוִד בְּכָל תְּפִלּוֹתָיו

analysis_notes.gap_analysis: Torah #279 is a short teaching (4 sentences) but it contains rich explicit bechina language. The Rebbe uses 'בִּבְחִינַת' / 'בִּבְחִינוֹת' three times in sentence 3 alone, building a bechina cluster around the shofar. The core bechina group is: שׁוֹפָר ↔ הִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִלְּמַטָּה ↔ 'וְדִבֶּר פִּי בַּצַּר לִי' ↔ מֵצַר (the narrow place). These four concepts are all expressions of the same structural reality: beginning compressed/narrow from below, opening wide above. David's prayer (תְּפִלָּה מִן הַמֵּצַר) is the concrete human embodiment of this pattern. The arrival at רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ is the eitza destination — distress PRODUCES divine inspiration, but distress and divine inspiration are NOT bechinat of each other. The two Torah-teaching archetypes (מלמטה למעלה / מלמעלה למטה) in sentences 1–2 are structural background concepts, described without bechina language, but they motivate the teaching. The 'holy spark' (נִיצוֹץ הַקָּדוֹשׁ) at the top of the narrowing teaching is a significant concept. None of these concepts currently exist in the dataset for this Torah; all must be added.
